citeAs: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li (2025). VoiceAssistant-Eval: Benchmarking AI Assistants Across Listening, Speaking, and Viewing. arXiv:2509.22651.
creator: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li (CUHK MMLab, SenseTime Research, CPII under InnoHK)
description: VoiceAssistant-Eval is a comprehensive benchmark designed to assess AI assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing. It comprises 10,497 curated examples spanning 13 task categories, including natural sounds, music, spoken dialogue for listening; multi-turn dialogue, role-play imitation, and various scenarios for speaking; and highly heterogeneous images for viewing. The benchmark evaluates both the quality of response content and speech, as well as their consistency.
name: VoiceAssistant-Eval
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human evaluation validation was conducted on 10% of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B's responses (1,050 examples) across all 13 tasks. Pearson correlation coefficients between automated (gpt-oss-20b) and human evaluations ranged from 0.73 to 1.00, with an overall correlation of 0.92. Agreement rates were uniformly high (often above 90%), with an overall agreement rate of 96.1%. Evaluation stability was also tested by repeating scoring 10 times, showing low variance (standard deviations mostly below 3).
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom web-based curation tool built by the authors
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A multi-stage curation process was used: (1) Deduplication using lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance to flag potential duplicates, which were manually reviewed and removed; (2) Validation to exclude incomplete or unsuitable instances (corrupted images, silent audio, ill-posed prompts, incorrect answers) — approximately 10% of candidates were discarded; (3) Categorization assigning problems to 13 predefined task categories based on source metadata; (4) Sampling to balance the ratio of different tasks. A web-based curation tool was built to standardize quality checks, with curators assigning Good or Bad verdicts per item.
rai:dataBiases: The benchmark is primarily in English (monolingual focus), with only five Chinese roles in the role-play task, which may not capture the full variability of real user interactions. Questions and contexts are drawn from academic or synthetic sources (existing datasets and rewritten instructions), which might not reflect the full richness or fairness concerns of real deployments. The role-play subset uses a fixed set of 100 roles that may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas. The evaluation relies on automated measures and GPT-based scoring, which may introduce noise and bias.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from 47 source datasets spanning audio and visual modalities. For the Listening subset, source data was drawn from 23 audio understanding datasets covering speech, sound, music, and general audio. For the Speaking subset, data came from 22 datasets including 11 text datasets and 11 audio datasets, plus role profiles from RoleBench. For the Viewing subset, MMMU was used as the source dataset spanning 30 disciplines and 30 image formats.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of audio clips (natural sounds, music, speech, dialogue), images from diverse domains, and text from existing datasets. Source datasets include LibriSpeech, Common Voice, Clotho, AudioCaps, AVQA, MusicCaps, MUSIC-AVQA, MMMU, RoleBench, and 38 other datasets totaling 47 source datasets.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is primarily in English (monolingual), limiting generalizability to diverse linguistic settings. The benchmark evaluates models in an offline, static manner and does not measure reaction time, handling of partial utterances, barge-in, or error recovery. Video-audio integration and continuous audio-visual streaming tasks are not covered. The range of evaluated models is limited, with only one proprietary system (GPT-4o-Audio). The dataset should not be used for training models for cheating.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Speech instructions were synthesized using three TTS models (F5TTS, ChatTTS, Dia-1.6B) to replace original text instructions. 300 role audio clips from the role-play task were reused as prompt audio to increase speaker diversity. Balanced sampling was applied to equalize category representation across 13 task categories. In total, 13,471 high-quality speech audio files were synthesized.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text preprocessing for TTS synthesis included: (1) replacing image reference tokens with descriptive phrases; (2) rewriting text using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct to make it suitable for TTS (e.g., converting mathematical expressions and numbers to spoken form); (3) rephrasing multiple-choice options for better readability. Speech quality was evaluated with UTMOS Strong and only clips scoring above 3.8 were retained. Whisper-Large-v3 was used to transcribe synthesized audio, and only the sample with the lowest word error rate was kept.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark includes role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation, raising concerns about identity spoofing, harassment, and fraud. Safeguards include: prohibiting training or releasing models intended to reproduce identifiable speakers without consent; requiring downstream users to implement consent gating and watermarking; providing safety cards describing acceptable use, known risks, and red-team tests for voice cloning abuse. A data governance process for auditing and removal is maintained.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating AI voice assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing capabilities; benchmarking multimodal models on audio understanding, speech generation, and audio-visual integration; tracking progress toward next-generation AI assistants; facilitating future studies in voice assistant development.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: F5TTS, ChatTTS, and Dia-1.6B (TTS models for speech synthesis); UTMOS Strong (speech quality evaluation); Whisper-Large-v3 (transcription for WER-based selection); Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (text rewriting for TTS); gpt-oss-20b (automated content quality evaluation); emotion2vec (emotion probability estimation); Wespeaker (speaker similarity calculation)
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The benchmark includes speaker voice profiles (100 distinct roles with 3 audio clips each) that could be used for voice imitation. The dataset involves speaker similarity evaluation which raises privacy concerns around voice identity.

evidence.name: We introduce VoiceAssistant-Eval , a comprehensive benchmark designed to assess AI assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing.
evidence.description: VoiceAssistant-Eval comprises 10,497 curated examples spanning 13 task categories. These tasks include natural sounds, music, and spoken dialogue for listening; multi-turn dialogue, role-play imitation, and various scenarios for speaking; and highly heterogeneous images for viewing.

evidence.inLanguage: Although we include five Chinese roles in the role-play task, all other prompts and evaluations are in English. This monolingual focus may not capture the full variability of real user interactions.
evidence.license: The VoiceAssistant-Eval data and our open-source code are under an MIT license.
evidence.isLiveDataset: VoiceAssistant-Eval evaluates models in an offline, static manner, which might not capture certain practical deployment factors.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: When collecting test data, we first extract diverse visual and auditory inputs from 37 datasets, including natural sounds, music, dialogue, and various images. To evaluate voice personalization, we utilize texts from RoleBench (Wang et al., 2023c) and analyze both role-specific speaking style and vocal timbre, thereby demonstrating the model's potential for personalized interactions.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: When collecting test data, we first extract diverse visual and auditory inputs from 37 datasets, including natural sounds, music, dialogue, and various images.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Tab. 8 provides an overview of the diverse set of source datasets included in our benchmark. For each dataset, we list the number of samples incorporated into VoiceAssistant-Eval . This comprehensive collection spans a wide variety of tasks and modalities, ensuring a thorough and balanced evaluation across different domains.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We preprocess the texts to ensure high synthesis quality: 1. Image references: We replace special tokens (e.g., "<image1>") with descriptive phrases, such as "as shown in the first image." 2. Text rewriting: We use Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025) to rewrite the text so it is more suitable for TTS, ensuring that challenging content, such as numbers and mathematical expressions, is read accurately.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: We improve data quality through a four-stage curation process: (1) Deduplication: We use lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance to flag potential duplicate questions. Suspected duplicates are manually reviewed and removed, resulting in 15,359 samples. (2) Validation: We exclude incomplete or unsuitable instances, including entries with corrupted images, silent audio, ill-posed prompts, and demonstrably incorrect answers. Approximately 10% of candidates are discarded at this stage.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: To operationalize the validation step described in the main text, we build a lightweight web-based curation tool that standardizes quality checks across modalities. The tool ingests candidate items consisting of a unique ID, metadata, raw prompt, reference answer(s), and associated media (audio waveform(s), image(s), and optional multi-turn transcripts).
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: During speech synthesis, we use UTMOS Strong (Saeki et al., 2022) to evaluate the generated speech and regenerate it until the score surpasses 3.8. To increase speaker diversity, we reuse the 300 role audio clips from the role-play task as prompt audio. Finally, we use Whisper-Large-v3 (Radford et al., 2022) to transcribe the synthesized audio back into text and select the audio sample with the lowest word error rate. In total, we synthesize 13,471 high-quality speech audio files.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We synthesize speech for question texts using three advanced text-to-speech (TTS) models: F5TTS (Chen et al., 2024b), ChatTTS (Team, 2025), and Dia-1.6B (Sung et al., 2025). evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We intend for researchers to use this dataset to better evaluate voice assistants and, consequently, facilitate future studies in this area.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Fourth, like many benchmarks, VoiceAssistant-Eval may carry biases from its source data and design choices. The questions and contexts are drawn from academic or synthetic sources (e.g., existing datasets and rewritten instructions), which might not reflect the full richness or fairness concerns of real deployments. For example, the role-play subset uses a fixed set of 100 roles and associated style prompts. These roles may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: VoiceAssistant-Eval evaluates models in an offline, static manner, which might not capture certain practical deployment factors. Real-world voice assistants operate under latency constraints, continuous listening requirements, and sometimes involve incremental speech processing. Our current evaluation does not measure reaction time, the ability to handle partial utterances, or how well a model can manage barge-in (user interruption) and error recovery.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: In addition, because the benchmark includes role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation, we emphasize strict consent, provenance, and anti-impersonation safeguards. To mitigate misuse risks (e.g., identity spoofing, harassment, fraud), we (i) prohibit training or releasing models intended to reproduce identifiable speakers without documented consent; (ii) require downstream users to implement consent gating and watermarking or traceability of synthetic audio; (iii) provide "safety cards" that describe acceptable use, known risks, and red-team tests for voice cloning abuse.
evidence.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: To evaluate voice personalization, we utilize texts from RoleBench (Wang et al., 2023c) and analyze both role-specific speaking style and vocal timbre, thereby demonstrating the model's potential for personalized interactions. Specifically, we select 100 distinct roles and collect three representative audio clips per role.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Table 6 shows a very strong agreement between our automated model-based evaluation scheme (using gpt-oss-20b (OpenAI et al., 2025)) and human judgments across various tasks. All reported Pearson correlation coefficients between the model's scores and human ratings are notably high (ranging from 0.73 to 1.00, with an overall correlation of 0.92), indicating a strong linear relationship.
